speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: I wish to call the attention of the government, and the Minister of the Interior in particular, to a telegram-indeed more than one telegram- which I have received from Winnipeg protesting against certain concessions, or rather the promise of a concession, said to have been made in respect of certain pulpwood areas in northern Manitoba, especially to those features providing only for pulpwood manufacture on a small scale rather than paper manufacture-to both the smallness of the scale and the fact that only partial manufacture is to be made of the raw material- as inadequate compensation for the very large concessions given. I would ask the Minister if he would make any statement that he can on the subject, and also if he would lay on the table of the House the agreements or order in council, or both, whichever may exist.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I notice 'by press despatches that there has been considerable agitation about a concession granted to the Manitoba Pulp and Paper Company in Winnipeg, due largely, I think, to the fact that there is not a definite provision for the location of the mill in the city of Winnipeg. However, in reply to the question of my right hon. friend I would say

Pulpwood Concessions
that there is definite provision in the contract for the manufacture of both pulp and paper.

How much?
Mr. STEWART (Argenteuil) Fifty per cent of the product of the mill is to be manufactured into paper, and none of the pulp can be exported from Canada without the consent of the minister, so that there is definite provision for the manufacture of paper and the construction of a paper plant in connection with the pulp plant.
What is the extent of the plant?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
At present one hundred tons per day, but it can be extended to a two hundred ton plant which I am given to understand' is the economic unit. That is the definite provision. My information is that the city of Winnipeg are very anxious to secure this plant. But the difficulty in Winnipeg is the water supply, They require a very large supply of pure water which would have to be filtered, if taken from the river proper, or obtained from the greater Winnipeg water supply, whereas if the company located on lake Winnipeg or on the English river they would have these advantages besides being somewhat closer to their source of power. The project is to be undertaken with power developed by the Manitoba Power Company at its inception, and from a development of power later on. I submitted the agreement and order in council on the matter to the provincial government. The mayor and council-I would not sty the council but the mayor at all events-of the city of 'Winnipeg consulted with the members representing the district, and the features of the contract, I think, protect ev.-.ry one thoroughly. We have a deposit of $250,000 as a guarantee that the mill will be started, but no cutting will be permitted until $1,000,000 has been expended upon the mill itself. In addition, there is a perpetual bond of $175,000 for the faithful performance of the contract. The citizens of Winnipeg, and of Manitoba generally, have been extremely anxious for a long time to have this industry established, and it is in compliance with that request that the agreement was entered into with the Manitoba Pulp and Paper Company for_ the carrying out of the project. The territory available in Manitoba will warrant the construction of two mills, so far as we know at the present time, of two hundred ton capacity each. That is according to the information that we have from our Forestry department. The whole agreement and contract have been
fully scrutinized and will be found, I think, eminently satisfactory. I shall be very glai to lay the order in council and the contract upon the table of the House on Monday.

This is to carry out a

This is an amendment suggested by the Chief Electoral Officer with a view of overcoming one of the difficulties referred to in the quotation from his 1922 report in the note to section 5 of the billl. In that report lie says with regard to this amendment:-
''The only way in which it appears possible consistently with the proper protection of the voter to render easier the removail of the names of dead and disqualified voters from the preliminary lists for urban polling divisions is to create a new class of applications to the revising officer in which the onus of establishing qualification is placed upon the voter
concerned instead of upon the applicant. When the onus rests upon the applicant it is exceedingly difficult to discharge, and experience indicates that, except when, as has happened, the machinery is used with the apparently deliberate purpose of blocking the revision, it is almost never resorted to. At the same time, it is impossible to allow the onus to be generally placed upon the voter without any responsibility upon the applicant, since the inevitable effect of so doing would be to put into the power of unscrupulous partisans not only to make the revision of the lists in the time available an impossibility, but to impose upon all their political opponents and unjustifiable burden. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I asked the
minister in charge of the bill to hold this section for the moment. I have sent to get information covering the last twenty years as to the length of time that has elapsed between the day of officially announcing the election and polling day, because I think that information would be of interest and helpful to the committee in deciding this mater. Last night in the discussion which took place a great deal was said about the interest of individual candidates in different ridings, but nothing or very little was said with respect to the public interest and the desirability of not keeping business in this country in an unsettled condition over a long period of time. That, I believe, is the reason why in Great Britain and other countries the time fixed is as short as it can be. Everyone knows that during the period of an election, business becomes greatly unsettled. Large business concerns will not place orders, banks more or less suspend a part of their loaning operations, and generally the whole business of the country is unsettled through the period in which the politi-[DOT] cal campaign takes place. The government in seeking to shorten the period of time had this in mind and more particularly the confusion of the last election when over a quarter of the year was taken up in an election campaign, in so acting we believe we are furthering the best interest of the country primarily and doing what will prove to be in the interest of candidates themselves. It must be remembered that a political campaign does not necessarily start the moment the announcement of an election is made. The people of the country are judging a government from the moment it takes office, and all through the year constituencies are being addressed by members and candidates. When my hon
Elections Act

friends return to the west the first thing they will do, I imagine, will be to visit different parts of their constituencies and express their views on the political questions of the day. So the limiting of time does not mean that political discussion is being confined within these limits. It is simply that the country may know that for a certain period, and only for that period, will the necessary turmoil of a political contest be kept up.
However, as I have said, the reason for holding this section for the moment is to get the further information I have sent for; and I think if we discover by it that it has been possible to hold elections in this country for a number of years in a shorter period of time, that ought to be some guide to the committee in settling this matter. Again I would say 'that the period of forty-five days is from the point of view of the Chief Electoral Officer only, what in his opinion could happen under the most favourable circumstances assuming that there is no hitch in any particular. That is the minimum, but it does not mean that the election may not take a very much longer time.

My reason for rising to
speak a moment ago was that this section is going to shorten the time between nomination and polling day to one week in most of the constituencies, and I am sure that that will be too short. It is simply inviting trouble, because in many of the constituencies it will be found almost impossible to print the ballots and distribute them to outlying polls within one week, and it may result in many elections having to be fought all over again. To-day we are asked to move that commission to Winnipeg. The report shows that between 1911 and 1919 the overages amounted in value to ten million dollars, or a million dollars a year.

I am not criticizing the elevator companies at the head of the lakes, because these overages are a legitimate gain to them according to the handling of grain in this country under our law.
Mr". SALES: There are over four thousand country elevators west of Winnipeg, The hon. member says that all the overages take place at the head of the lakes; I would say they do not.

All the overages at
the terminal elevators originate in the country elevators.

I am simply suggesting that all these overages take place in the first instance at the country elevators.

We cannot very well have the grain commissioners at every country elevator, but we can have them at the elevators at the head of the lakes where eighty-five per cent of the grain of western Canada is handled. I am pointing out that at the head of the lakes is where the Board of Grain Commissioners should be, the point where the screenings, overages, and all the other handling of grain takes place. I am trying to convince my hon. friends that in their own interest that is where the board should be stationed. Mr. Maharg said in the course of the same speech in 1919 that if a large overage is taken, it is just that much taken from the farmer.

Does the hon. member
realize that the farmers of the west are awake to the importance of this screening business and are going to have cleaners on their threshing machines and keep the screenings at home?

I am very glad to hear that on behalf of the farmers. But I notice the Royal Grain Commission did not recommend that, and in the discussion before the committee many members did not agree that it could be done profitably at home. Many of the country elevators, and many of the

threshing machines, have cleaners, but they are only used to the extent of five per cent, according to the report.

It is not the elevators,

I would recommend that that be done, especially if you are going to move the Board of Grain Commissioners from the head of the lakes to Winnipeg.
Then in regard to mixing, which will be done under this act-I have forgotten the particular section for the moment-it will be done at the head of the lakes.
4 p.m. Frankly, I am in favour of mixing, for I think it is in the interests of the prairie farmer, and I think the man who has a high-grade wheat and permits it to be mixed with a low-grade car and gets the higher value deserves that advantage Suppose you have two cars of wheat, one a go.; 1 No. 2 northern and the other a poor No. 2 northern, to-day the owner of the lower grade gets the same as the owner of the higher grade. So I believe mixing is a favourable thing for the western farmer. But all that mixing will take place at the head of the lakes where the Board of Grain Commissioners should be. In other words, I have tried to demonstrate to this committee that that is the point where the western farmer can get more use out of the Board of Grain Commissioners than at any other point in western Canada. If the Board of Grain Commissioners look after the interests of the western farmers, as I think they try to do, that is where they can do so to the best advantage.
According to the report of one of the commissioners, ninety per cent of the disputes take place west of Winnipeg. Perhaps that is so; I do not dispute his honesty, but I doubt if his estimate is correct. I admit that if you take into account all the letters dealing with little disputes at the small country elevators perhaps the estimate is correct, but I submit that many a question arising at the head of the lakes is as important as five hundred disputes at the country elevators.
Then, there may be disputes at country elevators; disputes as to leaks in cars, but these are mostly dealt with at the head of the lakes, and the report of the gram commissioners for 1924 shows that for that year there were 31,3S2 leaking cars to be investigated, and 14,112 cars with defective seals had to be investigated. to be dealt with at the head of the lakes. As to shortages on cars going into the elevators, Mr. Searle, the chief weighmaster, says, "We still have a large number." Then shortages on the outturn cargoes off boats are of the utmost importance, and Mr. Searle says that "a number of serious individual shortages were reported". And on page 13 it is stated *that one case was settled for 4,170 bushels of wheat, which is a rather large amount.
Bad grading has also to be corrected at the head of the lakes. The commission must not only visit the farmers of the prairie provinces, but visit also Ottawa and the other elevators which have been placed under their supervision-the elevators of Quebec, Montreal, St. John and Halifax, all of which have been put under the supervision of the board. That is all the more reason for keeping the board where they can reach the elevators more easily than they can from Winnipeg.
I should also like to quote from an independent paper, one at all events that cannot be accused of being favourable to the head of the lakes, the Calgary Herald, and I hope my hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Shaw) will pay attention to this, and follow the advice of the Calgary Herald.

I am afraid that I cannot
take much stock in it.

This is a paper published in the city of my hon. friend. I did not know its politics, but apparently I do now. The Calgary Herald is firmly opposed to the removal of the commission from Fort William. Commenting upon the vote of the committee on Agriculture, the Herald says:
Parliament should not hastily accept the recommendation of the agricultural committee concerning the transfer of the board of grain commissioners from Fort William to Winnipeg.
At Fort William the commissioners are at the scene of the largest terminal elevating work in the world and they can exert a direct and beneficial influence there. They would live too much in the atmosphere of the grain exchange at Winnipeg.
Might I point out that the Calgary Herald is owned by a Montreal firm?
That does not make it favourable to Fort William as opposed to Winnipeg.
The ownership is vested in a concern in Montreal.

I do not know anything about who owns the paper. I do not see that has anything to do with the question, as long as this is not a paper owned by somebody in Fort William.

Canada Grain Act
The mixing of our wheat, and the vicious mixing of it with grains of lower grades, can take place anywhere from the head of the lakes right down to the point where the grain leaves New York and other American ports. That is an important question from the standpoint of the reputation of our Canadian grain, and a question that should be considered from the standpoint of the grain handler, not of the grain seller.
It has been claimed that the Board of Grain Commissioners have not been visiting the farmers at all. That is up to the farmers. If they demand a visit of the board in connection with any dispute they may have, they have a right to have the Board of Grain Commissioners to visit them, and the board can visit them just as well from the head of the lakes as from Winnipeg.
In 1912, when the Grain Act was originally drawn up, the Board of Grain Commissioners was placed at the head of the lakes, after due consideration had been given to the question by the Department of Trade and Commerce and by the then chairman of the Board of Grain Commissioners. The board has been located there for thirteen years, and during those thirteen years no real move has ever been made to change its location. If there had been any dissatisfaction with the present location of the board, surely some move would have been made before now. My hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) is of the opinion that the board should be moved to Winnipeg. He has been in this House as long as I have, eight years, and if there was any dissatisfaction it was open to him to move an amendment to the Canada Grain Act at any session of parliament foi the purpose of having the board removed from the head of the lakes to Winnipeg. In 1919, when amendments to the Canada Grain Act were brought into this House, no amendment was proposed at that time to change the location of the commission, so that if the farmers have not been getting justice, it ia a strange thing that no move has been made in all that time, to move the Board of Grain Commissioners from the head of the lakes.
Again, if this step is necessary, why did not the Royal Grain Commission, which sat on this question and held meetings throughout Canada for nearly two years, recommend that the board should be moved to Winnipeg? All they had to recommend on this point was that the board should be an itinerant or travelling board. Two or more of the commissioners can be in Winnipeg at any time. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) when he was arguing against me in the

committee, spoke about inspection; he dragged inspection in by the neck, as it were, * for it has nothing to do with moving the board from the head of the lakes to Winnipeg. He argued as if I was trying to move the Inspection department from Winnipeg to the head of the lakes. No such proposal has ever been made. The inspection would remain where it is at the present time.
Then there is also the question of economy. To move the board, you would have to move something over one hundred people. I do Dot mean the employees but the families, and at present costs that expense would be a heavy one upon the government -of this country.
Now I wish to give a moral reason. In 1912 when this board was placed at the head of the lakes, it was placed there after Sir George Foster, then Minister of Trade and Commerce, had consulted with the mayor and people of the city of Fort William and had asked them to erect a building for a sample market and for the Board of Grain Commissioners. The proper accommodation was discussed with Mr. Magill, the dhairman of the board, and the building was put up by individual subscriptions of the people of the city to Fort William to the amount of $500.000. That was subscribed in 1912, when conditions were pretty bad. And despite the fact that they did that, no sample market was ever placed there, though the building was cut up for it. As a consequence, these individuals who subscribed have received no dividends on their money until the last two or three years, when they have been receiving dividends of only 2 or 2i per cent. There is a spirit of British fair play in this country which should see to it that a government which had an understanding of that kind with the city of Fort William should not be able to ignore it as the Germans ignored their treaties with Belgium and other countries, regarding them as no more than scraps of paper.
Then, in regard to the revenue of the board. The board took in in 1924, according to their own report, $1,787,000, and of that, $1,095,000 was taken in at-the head of the lakes; that is, two-thirds of the whole revenue in 1924 was taken in at the head of the lakes, the balance was taken in all the way from Vancouver to Montreal. Even the inspection fees, the report shows, were more at the head of the lakes than at Winnipeg, The weighing fees were $668,000. Weighing is a very important thing to the farmers of western Canada. Weighing, of course, is done at the country elevators also, but the weighing

Canada Grain Act
into the terminal elevators is naturally done at the head of the lakes. In other words, practically every branch of the work of handling grain is done at that point.
I have tried to show that Fort William, at the head of the lakes, is the link, and an important link, in the chain of the handling of grain in Canada. I do not believe the farmers of the prairie provinces who have taken this attitude in favour of Winnipeg are working in their own interests. Even in the committee ther'e was not a set decision upon it. There were two amendments which I hold in my hand. One was that the board be moved to Winnipeg. That was wiped out by the committee itself, and the following substituted therefor:
The head office of the board shall be at the city of Winnipeg. The Governor in Council may upon the recommendation of the board from time to time establish offices of the board at other places.
So there was doubt in the committee as to the advisability of the move.
I just wish to say, in closing, that the people of my city are too broad-minded to take any attitude which would be detrimental to Canada as a whole. I have never made it my duty to take parochial views in this House. Take, for example, the question of the shipment of grain west to the port of Vancouver. Of course, the more grain goes west, the greater the injury to Fort William, but I have never made any attempt in this House to interfere with that movement in any way, either on the question of railway rates or anything else. The same is true with regard to the Hudson Bay railway. Although I have grave doubts as to the wisdom of building that road, I have never spoken in oppositon to it because I did not wish to be accused of taking an attitude opposed to the west simply on behalf of my own city. I think this question should be approached in the spirit in which I have endeavoured to approach questions in this House. It should be approached from the standpoint of the prairie provinces, and from the standpoint of justice and fair play. I appeal particularly to my friends in the Progressive group to look at this question in a fair-minded way, and to leave the board at the head of the lakes at least for another year, and then if there is any dissatisfaction they can bring in an amendment next session to move the board from the head of the lakes. I appeal to them and the House generally to give fair and just consideration to this question, and to leave the board at the head of the lakes, where I think they are most. useful not only to the grain trade but to Canada as a whole.

When the board were first created in 1912, the reason, if I recall aright, that was given why they should be located at the head of the lakes was that they would be removed from any possibility of temptation from the organized grain trade at Winnipeg. I do not think there was any virtue in that reason, because if you had a board composed of honest and honourable

Canada Grain Act
men who were sworn to discharge their duty they could scarcely be influenced by the organized grain trade. If there was any virtue in the suggestion I submit it does not hold to-day.
This is another generation.

Yes, the world is making
progress, and I can tell my hon. friend he will see it one of these days. Everyone will admit that the grain business of this country is one of the great businesses of the Dominion. In its growth and development it has been found, in the public interest, not only in the interests of the producers of grain, but in the national interests as well, that we should have certain legislative sanctions for the governing and control of the trade. In order that those legislative sane ions might be carried out as effectively as possible in the interests of the producers, and in the national interests as well, the Board of Grain Commissioners was created for the purpose of administering the law. The fundamental principle of the Grain Act is the regulation of the trade.
